grade_about_1: Five-finger tunes that stay in one hand position — steady quarter and half notes, nothing to stretch for.
grade_about_2: A little hand movement and simple two-hand coordination; mostly steps with the odd small skip.
grade_about_3: Both hands working together more, slightly wider reaches, and the first dotted rhythms and eighth-note runs.
grade_about_4: Position shifts, simple chords, and phrases that ask each hand to do something of its own.
grade_about_5: Faster passages, fuller chords, and accidentals that pull you out of the home key.
grade_about_6: Independent hands throughout, broader leaps, and ornaments or syncopation to hold in time.
grade_about_7: Demanding two-hand textures, quick position changes, and dense rhythms at a real tempo.
grade_about_8: Concert-level pieces — rapid runs, big stretches, and the full range of the keyboard.
about_intro: Plinky is made by two people who think learning the piano should feel like playing — never a chore.
about_sol_bio: Sol is the creative force behind our brand. She handles our marketing and works hard behind the scenes to ensure you love every moment with Plinky.
about_sebastian_bio: Sebastian writes the code — the notation, the ear drills, the thousand small details — turning the vision into something you can sit down and play.
about_why_body: We wanted a calm place to play. No streaks to break, no leaderboard to climb — just you, a keyboard, and the next note. And we were set on making sure everyone can play it — whatever their device, however they get around a screen. Every piece in the library is Creative Commons, credited to the people who wrote it.
about_contact_body: Questions, a piece you'd love to see, or just to say hi — we're always glad to hear from you. Drop us an email, or find us on social.
meta_about_description: Meet the two people behind Plinky — and why they built a calmer way to learn the piano.
help_intro: How Plinky works, area by area — have a look wherever you're curious.
help_text_intro:
Plinky is a piano trainer that turns practice into a game. You read the notes on the screen, play them, and Plinky says how it went. Everything runs in your browser — nothing is uploaded, your progress stays on your own device, and there is no account to make.

There are no version numbers here either. New builds install themselves quietly and only take over between pages, or when you come back to the tab — never in the middle of a run.
help_text_getting_started:
Nothing here is locked, so there is no order you have to follow. Open Plinky and Today already knows what to offer: a first piece to play, the day's challenge, and one thing to learn. Press any of them.

Under it sits a short Getting started strip with the three things that tailor everything after them — connecting a digital piano (or letting Plinky listen through the microphone), telling Plinky how far your hands reach, and choosing which computer keys play which notes. It goes away for good once they are done, or when you dismiss it.

Never played a piano at all? Learn opens with Meet the keyboard: six short steps, no cable and no reading needed.
help_text_home:
Today is where you land, and it holds the day's practice in the shape a piano teacher gives an hour.

Warm up offers the day's challenge, your next rung of the sight-reading arcade, a fresh drill and a round of ear training. Work on carries the next step of an open assignment — which jumps straight into that piece — whatever is fading and wants a refresh, and the gentlest piece you have not learned yet; Surprise me picks one for you. Learn one thing offers a single lesson, mark or method, chosen for the day.

They are headings rather than a list of chores. Nothing counts them, nothing ticks them off, and skipping one costs you nothing.
help_text_play:
Open any piece from Music, or one you imported, and Plinky engraves it as real notation. One button leads the way: Practice.

Every play page has two tabs — Play, the score and everything you do with it, and Runs, your saved performances. Practice drops you into full screen, just the score and the keyboard with the screen kept awake, and starts a note-by-note guide: read the note, play it, and the cursor moves on, sounding the note back the way you played it. A quick tap plays staccato, a held key sustains, and how hard you strike sets how loud it is. A MIDI piano, the on-screen keys and your computer keyboard all work, and no pedal is needed.

The controls in full screen: Listen plays the piece so you hear it first and hands off to Practice mid-phrase; Set up slides in the same panel you get before a run; Restart takes the run back to the top; the X leaves full screen, keeping your place; and Finger positions swaps the keyboard for the fingering editor.

Listen and Practice hand off to each other in both directions — let the computer play a tricky passage and take over mid-phrase, or play a while and hand it back. Your place is always kept.

As you play, the score keeps a record of how the run went. Blue is what the computer played, green is what you read cleanly, and amber is a note you found only after a wrong key, which flashes red. So a finished piece shows exactly where you hesitated, instead of a uniform green that forgets.
help_text_play_setup:
Before a run — and behind the Set up button mid-piece — sits every reading aid and layout choice, grouped into cards.

Skill level is one choice that sets all the reading aids to match you; tweak any of them and it reads Custom. A new device starts at New starter, with every aid on.

How you play holds which hand you are practising (on a two-hand piece), whether Plinky fills in the hand you are not, keep-up, and the metronome. Reading aids holds note colour, the notes highway, hidden notes and finger numbers. Score layout holds follow-the-note scrolling, bars per row, treadmill reading, note size, bar numbers, beams, and other parts — which brings back a singer's or another instrument's staff, shown and sounded, never something you are asked to play. Extra challenge holds sight-reading, with a preview of 5, 10 or 20 seconds, and bars that disappear behind you as you leave them.

A few of those are worth knowing by name. The notes highway swaps the staff for a tall lane of falling notes coloured per hand, for seeing which key comes next without decoding the staff. Coloured notes make every C red and every D orange, so you read pitch by hue while the names sink in. Loop repeats the piece, or just a passage: tap two bars on the score and they fill red, or set the range by bar number, and Show only the looped bars re-engraves that stretch on its own, drawn big. Keep going means a missed note no longer freezes you — playing the next one moves the score along. Hidden notes start the noteheads blank for ear practice, revealing each as you find it. Finger positions opens the fingering editor, where every note arrives pre-fingered for your hand span and you can tap a note then a finger to override it, with bars washed red by fingering difficulty so the hard spots show. Keep up makes practice tempo-locked: after a one-bar count-in the cursor moves on the beat, ready or not.

Starting out: leave note colours and the notes highway on, slow things right down, and loop any bar that keeps tripping you up.

Further on: Sight-read this piece, under Extra challenge, steps every reading aid aside and gives you a few seconds to take the piece in, then one clean run. Your first read is saved as your sight-read and never overwritten.
help_text_play_grading:
When you finish, a short flourish plays and the run is graded S to F from three things: accuracy, how many notes you found cleanly; timing, how evenly you held the rhythm — judged against your own tempo, so a steady run at any speed reads as in time; and flow, whether you kept moving like a musician.

Where the music is marked, an Expression reading joins them, for how closely you followed the written dynamics and articulation. It never changes your letter grade.

Afterwards a per-note strip and a tempo graph show where you rushed or dragged, and you can race a ghost of your best run — or a friend's, shared by link.
help_text_library:
Music is everything there is to play, in two tabs, plus Compose for music you make yourself.

Search is for finding something to play: search by name, star favourites, filter by kind, grade or what is due now, then open a piece. It comes stocked with scales, arpeggios, familiar tunes like Twinkle, Twinkle and Ode to Joy, and hundreds of real pieces, each credited with its composer, source and licence.

Manage is for growing and safeguarding it: add your own MusicXML scores by dropping them in, download a backup of your imports — or of the whole library, Plinky's own pieces included — and restore one.
help_text_learn:
Learn is the teaching side of Plinky, gathered in the order you meet it.

Meet the keyboard is six steps for someone who has never touched one. How the music works is a short course on what a stave is telling you, each lesson with something to play. What the marks mean explains every symbol you meet in a score, most of them with a button that plays the music with the mark and again without it. Ear training names what you hear, for the days you are nowhere near a piano.

Then the practising itself: Assignments is an ordered set of pieces — a teacher's, or one you build — with each step ticked off as you learn it, and Collect results reads the codes a student sends back. Ways to practise names six things a teacher would suggest and hands you the control that does each one. Little tools is the look-it-up bench: a circle of fifths, a scale and chord explorer, and a tap-tempo reader. Find your level reads a few generated drills and says which grade you actually read at.
help_text_daily:
One freshly generated phrase, the same for everyone that day, graded and shareable as a grid. Play it whenever you like — there is no streak to keep up, and a day you have not played arrives as a little present to open.

The Warm up tab shapes unlimited fresh phrases of your own: key signature (any of 15, or every note in the octave), range across the 88 keys, one hand or two, chords of up to four notes, note values, a cap on the biggest jump, and a stay-close toggle. Nothing here is memorisable — every setting makes fresh notation on the spot.

The Export menu on the title line prints, or downloads MIDI or MusicXML.

Starting out: the Warm up tab with a small range and single notes builds confidence before the main challenge.
help_text_ear:
A page of its own for the days you are nowhere near a piano. Intervals name the distance between two notes on a ladder; Chords name a chord's quality; Scales name which scale played; Chord progressions name each chord by its Roman numeral; the functional exercises cover scale degrees, intervals in context and melodic dictation; and Perfect pitch names a single note on a keyboard.

A round is ten questions, and finishing one counts toward your grades just as playing a piece does. A miss shows you what played rather than marking you down.

Starting out: Intervals begins on fifths and octaves and fills in from there.
help_text_compose:
Play whatever you like — on a MIDI piano, your computer keys or the on-screen keyboard — and Plinky records every note and sketches it onto a staff as you go. The playback is exactly what you played; the staff is an approximate sketch, snapped to a grid so it reads as notation.

Count in drops into full screen, the only place the on-screen keys appear here, with a one-bar count-in. There is a metronome to play along to, and a checkpoint to keep the good part and retry the tail. A take can be shared by link or downloaded as MIDI or MusicXML, and a MIDI or MusicXML file opens back up here, so you can pick up where you left off on another device.

Writing your own: checkpoints build a piece section by section, and the MusicXML export carries it into your notation software for the details.
help_text_assignments:
An ordered practice list, for a student or for yourself. A built-in First steps set for beginners is ready to play on day one.

To build your own: browse or search the catalogue, add pieces, drag them into order, and give each an optional target tempo and note. The whole set can carry a date you are working toward — a lesson, an exam, a recital — and its card counts down. Save it, edit it, share it by link or pass it around as a file; each piece checks off as it is learned.

For teachers: students hand results back by typing a name, which turns their device's progress into one code to paste into a message. Collect results reads those codes as a class table and downloads a CSV — it replaces transcription, not trust, and it is not proof. Assignments can also go out straight into Google Classroom.
help_text_you:
Your one progress page. It shows the grade you are at on the eight-grade ladder and what is left to reach the next, your skill rating, days practised and notes played, a slow-moving fingerprint of your accuracy, timing and flow, and the pieces due for review with a one-tap session.

You will also find Find your level, the placement test; the notes you take longest to find, which names the handful that consistently slow you down; Your practice, a diary rolled up over a week, a month, three months or a year with a shading grid showing where the practice went, where you can add hand-logged minutes and download the log as a spreadsheet; On the music stand, what you are working on and each piece's stage — learning, settling in, polishing, keeping it; and Achievements, every grade and badge you have earned, with the unearned ones shown as goals.

Gaps are fine. Plinky never counts streaks and never reproaches a missed day: a quiet week is simply drawn as a quiet week.
help_text_review:
Once you clear a piece it enters spaced repetition, resurfacing on a widening schedule so that what you learn actually sticks. A one-tap review session walks you through everything that is fading, and anything you are not working on right now can be shelved. Ear-training exercises join the same queue.

The schedule is worth trusting: mixing pieces in one session is one of the six methods teachers recommend, which you can read about under Ways to practice.
help_text_settings:
Where you make Plinky yours: pick and set up your instrument, tune the reading aids, say what counts as learned, and keep your progress safe.

Your instrument. Connect MIDI takes a digital piano over USB or Bluetooth and reconnects on its own next visit (Chrome, Edge and Firefox on desktop or Android — Safari and iOS have no Web MIDI). For an acoustic, or any piano at all, Start listening uses the microphone instead and works everywhere, iOS included; Tune to your piano is a short guided wizard — middle C, then a soft note and a firm one — that learns your room's noise floor, octave and loudness, and is worth running once per device.

On a computer keyboard, any playing key can be remapped. Out of the box the bottom row is the left hand — Z X C V B N M white, S D G H J black — and the top row the right — Q W E R T Y U white, 2 3 5 6 7 black — with an octave shift. Any unused key, the space bar included, can be bound to the sustain, sostenuto or soft pedal. The on-screen piano's width — one, two or three octaves, or the whole piece at once — sits in the practice tools on the play page.

Reading aids. Show the next note to play lights the keys to press and hints at how long to hold them, and can be set to always, only after a wrong key, or never. Note names on keys shows every key, only the Cs as landmarks, or none — and reads as do-re-mi in the languages where those are the real note names. Skill level and every reading preference live here too, matching the run panel: the ready-made combinations are New starter, Learning, Confident and Sight-reader, and changing anything makes it your own. Bars per row and note size find the fit for your screen; beams, racing your ghost and hidden notes come into their own further along. There is a metronome for when keeping time is the thing you are working on.

Starting out: keep the next note showing until a piece is familiar, then switch to after a mistake; keep the note names on the keys until the map is second nature, then drop to the Cs as landmarks. New starter with the beams hidden is a good place to begin. Telling Plinky how far each hand reaches also makes the suggested finger positions fit you.

Piano lights. If your piano lights its own keys, Follow along on my keyboard mirrors the notes as Plinky plays them during Listen, and Light the keys I'm about to play lights what is coming — Casio's MIDI In Navigate and Yamaha's Light Guide both work. Test the lights checks that everything agrees. Both are off until you ask for them.

What counts as learned. Every run is graded S, A, B, C or D, and Mastery is the lowest grade you want to count as learned. The grade settings say how gently or how strictly Plinky treats a piece you have been away from, and how many pieces a review session holds.

Your progress. Settings downloads everything as a single file — grades, review schedule, saved takes, fingerings, preferences, achievements and your score library — and restores it on another device exactly as it was. Restoring replaces what is on the device rather than merging, and always asks first. Nothing is stored online, so a backup file now and then is the only safety net if browser storage is ever cleared.
help_text_extras:
A few more corners worth exploring. How the music works is a short eight-lesson course on the theory the app assumes, each lesson with something to play. What the marks mean is a glossary of every notation symbol, each with a Hear it button — and the setup panel lists the marks your own piece uses. Little tools holds a circle of fifths, scale and chord explorers, and a tap-tempo reader. Ways to practice covers six teacher-approved techniques, each linking straight to the Plinky control that does it.

A few things worth knowing: Plinky installs from your browser like an app and works offline once loaded. If your device runs out of room or blocks saving, a banner says so — it never pretends a save landed when it did not. On an iPhone, silence usually means Silent Mode is on or the volume is down; opening Plinky from inside a social app blocks sound altogether, so open it in Safari instead. And the ? in the header opens this page on the section for wherever you came from.

meta_help_description: How Plinky works: guides for every part of the app, from your first note to tracking your progress.
meta_learn_description: Learn the piano in your browser: a keyboard tour for complete beginners, an eight-lesson theory course, a glossary of notation you can hear, ear training, and a few little tools.
basics_intro: Never played before? Six things, and you'll be playing notes on purpose. No piano needed — the keys below work fine.
meta_basics_description: A hands-on introduction to the piano keyboard for complete beginners: the black-key groups, middle C, the white keys, and how a note on the staff becomes a key under your hand.
tour_waiting: Try it on the keys — Next opens once you have.
tour_done_body: You can find any key from here. Everything else in Plinky builds on those six things — and they're all still true tomorrow.
tour_black_groups_title: The black keys come in twos and threes
tour_black_groups_body: That pattern repeats the whole way along, and it's how you find your place without counting. Press any black key.
tour_middle_c_title: Middle C sits left of a group of two
tour_middle_c_body: It's the landmark everything else is described from. Find a group of two black keys, and the white key just to its left is C. Press it.
tour_white_run_title: The white keys are seven letters, over and over
tour_white_run_body: Seven names, then they start over a little higher. Walk up all eight from middle C — the keys carry their names as you go.
tour_black_names_title: A black key has two names
tour_black_names_body: It sits between two white keys, so it's the higher one's flat and the lower one's sharp — one key, two names. Press the black key just right of middle C.
tour_note_to_key_title: A dot on the staff is a key under your hand
tour_note_to_key_body: This is how music is written down: the dot's height says which key. This one sits two white keys above middle C. Press it.
tour_high_low_title: Higher on the page, higher in sound
tour_high_low_body: Notes further up the staff are further right on the keys. Play the low one, then the high one.
score_symbols_subtitle: The marks you'll meet here, and what each one asks of you.
glossary_intro: The symbols you meet in a score, and what each one does to the sound. Most can be heard twice: as written, and again with the mark taken away.
glossary_example_unavailable: This example can't be drawn right now.
meta_glossary_description: A glossary of music notation: what every symbol in a score means, with an example you can hear.
glossary_dotted_gloss: The dot adds half the note's length again, so a dotted half note lasts three beats instead of two.
glossary_tie_gloss: A curve joining two notes of the same pitch. Play the first and hold it through the second — one sound, not two.
glossary_rest_gloss: A measured silence. The beat carries on; your hands don't.
glossary_staccato_gloss: A dot above or below the note: play it short and detached, releasing well before the next one.
glossary_accent_gloss: A wedge above the note: lean on it, so it arrives louder than the notes around it.
glossary_slur_gloss: A curve over notes of different pitches: play them joined, without a gap between them.
glossary_piano_gloss: Play softly. It's the Italian for soft — and where the instrument got its name.
glossary_forte_gloss: Play loudly, with some weight behind the note.
glossary_key_signature_gloss: The sharps or flats just after the clef apply to those notes all through the piece, without being marked again.
glossary_accidental_gloss: A sharp raises a note by a semitone, a flat lowers it, and a natural cancels either — for the rest of the bar.
glossary_time_signature_gloss: The two numbers after the key: the top one counts the beats in a bar, the bottom says which note gets one.
glossary_bass_clef_gloss: The lower staff's clef, usually your left hand. The same dot means a different key here than it would in the treble clef.
storage_write_failed: This device's storage is full or blocked — new progress isn't being saved.
sound_ios_hint: No sound? On iPhone, turn off Silent Mode (the side switch, or the Action button on newer models) and turn the volume up.
sound_inapp_hint: No sound here? This in-app browser blocks it — tap the ••• menu and choose Open in Safari.
coach_practice_loop: New here? Have a listen first, then play along as slowly as you like. If you slip, keep going — there's no need to start over.
transpose_caption: Changes the notes you play, not just the view
keep_up_hint: The score advances on the beat at a fixed tempo, and any note you don't catch in time slips by. A one-bar count-in leads you in.
guide_notes_hint: Each note sounds as it passes, so you can follow along. Turn it off to read them at tempo yourself.
duet_hint: The app plays the hand you're not practising, in time — so you play a duet with it.
keep_up_result: You kept up with {inTime} of {total} notes in time.
race_ghost_hint: A translucent replay of your best run on this piece plays alongside you.
rotate_hint: Turn your phone sideways for a bigger keyboard.
export_print_hint: Sheet music on paper — or save it as a PDF.
export_midi_hint: The notes as sound — for GarageBand, a DAW, or another practice app.
export_musicxml_hint: Editable notation — for MuseScore and other score editors.
loop_hint_narrow: tap two bars on the score to loop just a passage
tempo_trainer_caption: Nudges the tempo up a notch after each finished run, so you build speed a little at a time.
tempo_trainer_target_caption: The top speed the trainer climbs to before it stops nudging.
metronome_subdivision_caption: Clicks per beat — 1 on the beat, 2 for eighths, 3 for triplets, 4 for sixteenths.
hand_caption: Take a two-hand piece one hand at a time, or play both together.
loop_caption: Repeats the whole piece. For just a passage, tap two bars on the score (they turn red) — the range and controls appear right by the score.
fingering_show_mine_caption: Draws the fingering you saved for this piece onto the staff.
bars_per_row_caption: Forces this many bars onto each row for bigger notation; Auto fits them to your screen.
treadmill_hint: The piece reads as one line that scrolls as you play, instead of stacked rows.
accompaniment_hint: Some pieces are written for piano and a singer or another instrument. Their part stays out of the way unless you'd like to see and hear it alongside yours.
highway_hint: The notes to come stack above the keys and fall onto them as you play, so you can see which key is next.
highway_label: Upcoming notes falling onto the keys
bar_numbers_hint: Numbers the first bar of each row, so a passage is easy to find. Turn it off for a cleaner staff.
beams_caption: Beams join fast notes into beat groups. Hide them to read one note at a time while you're learning; Auto shows them on harder pieces, where the grouping helps.
note_size_caption: Magnifies the whole score for bigger, easier-to-read notes — handy on a small screen, or when you're starting out.
color_notes_hint: Each notehead takes a colour from its name — every C red, every D orange, and so on — so you can read by hue while the names sink in.
reading_level_help: Sets the reading aids together — pick where you are, then fine-tune any of them below.
reading_level_custom_help: Your own mix of aids. Pick a level to reset them.
settings_reading_hint: How the music reads while you play, and the aids that help you find the next note.
hand_size_instruction: tap your thumb key, then your pinky — or play them on a MIDI piano
home_eyebrow: Free · in your browser · nothing to install
home_keyboard_hint: Tap a key — that's a plink.
home_intro: Free, in-browser piano practice — no account, nothing to install. Bring a MIDI keyboard or use your computer keys, then play any score you like, or drill sight-reading, rhythm, tempo, and ear training. Every run is graded, and your scores and progress stay on your device.
perf_label: Each note placed by timing, ringed in red if the key was wrong, dashed if you hesitated
hands_even: Your hands kept pace with each other.
hand_left_lagged: Your left hand lagged a little behind your right.
hand_right_lagged: Your right hand lagged a little behind your left.
share_grid_label: How you played across six moments of the run, one row per hand
settings_mastery_threshold: Mark a score learned at grade
settings_mastery_help: A score counts as learned once a run reaches this grade, which schedules it for review. Lower the bar to mark scores learned sooner.
settings_decay_gentle_help: Your grades never drop — pieces just lose their shine until you refresh them. The kind default.
settings_decay_competitive_help: Neglected pieces can lapse, so a grade — and your skill rating — can actually slip. For bragging rights: a ⚔️ badge shows you're playing this way.
settings_review_cap_help: How many due pieces a review session offers in one go, so it stays a finishable batch rather than a pile.
play_compose_blurb: Improvise freely and Plinky catches every note, sketching your playing onto a staff you can share or take away as MusicXML or MIDI.
meta_compose_description: Improvise at the keyboard and Plinky sketches the notation — share your take or download it as MIDI or MusicXML
compose_intro: Play freely on a MIDI keyboard, your computer keys, or the keys below — Plinky catches every note and sketches it onto the staff. Count in to play along to the metronome for tidier notation, or set a checkpoint to keep the good part and retry the rest. Your take is yours to share or download, and a MIDI or MusicXML file opens right back up where you left off.
compose_staff_label: A staff sketch of your improvisation
compose_staff_empty: Play a few notes and they'll appear here.
compose_recording_idle: Recording — play anything, and every note is caught
compose_sketch_note: The audio is exactly what you played; the staff is an approximate sketch, snapped to a grid so it reads as notation.
compose_open_error: Couldn't read that file — a MIDI (.mid) or MusicXML (.musicxml, .mxl) file should open fine.
daily_intro: A new piece every day — the same one for everyone, a piano take on the daily puzzle. Give it a go, see how it lands, and share your grid if you'd like.
settings_subtitle: Your preferences stay on this device.
settings_show_fingerings: Show finger position hints while practising
settings_note_hints: Show the next note to play
settings_note_hints_help: A wrong key always flashes red. This sets when the correct key lights up — keeping it hidden leaves the reading to you.
settings_note_labels_help: Note names printed on the keys while you learn where they live. "Just C" marks only the C keys — the white key left of each pair of black keys — as a landmark to orient by.
settings_hand_size_hint: Tell Plinky how far you reach and the suggested finger positions follow your hands. With one hand, just set that one.
settings_get_help: Get help or report a bug
progress_backup_hint: Everything you've played lives on this device and nowhere else. A backup carries the lot — grades, saved takes, fingerings, settings and scores — to a new phone or laptop, or back here if this one is ever cleared.
progress_backup_restore_hint: Restoring replaces everything here with the backup.
progress_backup_error_unreadable: That file isn't a Plinky backup.
progress_backup_error_empty: That backup is empty — there's nothing to restore.
progress_backup_error_storage: This device's storage is full or blocked, so the restore didn't land. Nothing here has changed.

sight_read_tempo_caption: Your own pace waits for you; the piece's tempo doesn't.
sight_read_vanish_caption: Once you've played a bar it's gone, so your eyes stay ahead of your hands.

placement_intro: Read a drill; if it goes well the next one is harder. Three shaky ones and it stops. Nothing here is a piece you might already know — every drill is made on the spot.

placement_result_hint: That's where your reading sits today. It's a starting point, not a verdict — take it again whenever you like.

meta_ear_description: Name what you hear — intervals and single notes, straight in your browser. No piano, no sign-up, no cost.
home_ear_blurb: Away from the piano? Your ears can still practise — name the notes and the distances between them.
ear_intro: No piano needed here — just your ears and a quiet minute.
ear_level_help: Each one keeps the intervals before it and adds a few more.
ear_intervals_blurb: Two notes, one after the other. The rungs sit at the distance they name, so an answer has a height as well as a word.
ear_pitch_blurb: One note on its own, no clues — the keyboard is where you name it.
ear_verdict_close: Not that one — green is what played.
ear_session_recorded: That's a round done — it counts toward your grades.
ear_chords_blurb: A chord, all its notes at once. Name the quality you hear — the colour a chord has whatever its root.
ear_scales_blurb: A scale climbing from its tonic. Name which one it is by the pattern of steps.
ear_progressions_blurb: A run of chords in a key. Name each one you hear, in order — it starts and ends on the home chord, so the key is always there to hold onto.
ear_scale_degrees_blurb: A short cadence sets the key, then one note. Name where it sits in the key — the first degree, the third, the fifth?
ear_intervals_context_blurb: A cadence sets the key, then two notes. Name the interval between them, heard with the key to lean on.
ear_melodic_blurb: A cadence sets the key, then a little tune. Write it down degree by degree, in order.

datenschutz_controller_intro: The controller responsible for data processing on this website is:
datenschutz_short_body: Plinky is a browser-only application. Your settings, your progress and your recordings are stored only locally in your browser; we do not collect them or transmit them to a server. There are no user accounts, no advertising and no cookies. Visits are counted with a cookie-free measurement that stores nothing on your device and identifies nobody — so there is nothing here for you to consent to or switch off.
datenschutz_hosting_body: The website is delivered as static files via Cloudflare Pages (provider: Cloudflare, Inc., 101 Townsend St., San Francisco, CA 94107, USA). When the page is requested, the host processes technically necessary data such as your IP address, the date and time of access and the amount of data transferred, in order to deliver the page and keep operations secure. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in secure and stable delivery (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR). Any transfer to the USA relies on the provider's certification under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.
datenschutz_localstorage_body: To run the app we use your browser's local storage — for example for your settings, your practice progress and saved recordings. This data stays on your device, is not transmitted to us, and can be deleted at any time via the settings or your browser. The legal basis is Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (providing a functional, convenient app).
datenschutz_fonts_body: Fonts are loaded from our own server. No external services such as Google Fonts are used, so no data is transmitted to third parties in this respect.
datenschutz_analytics_body: To measure reach we use Cloudflare Web Analytics (provider: Cloudflare, Inc., 101 Townsend St., San Francisco, CA 94107, USA). It counts page views and measures loading speed without cookies, without local storage and without a fingerprint of your device; no data identifying you personally is processed, and there is no recognition across websites. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in the needs-based design of our website (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR); since no information is stored on or read from your device, § 25 TDDDG requires no consent. Further information can be found in Cloudflare's privacy policy.
datenschutz_email_body: If you write to us by email, we process the information you provide solely in order to handle your enquiry (Art. 6(1)(b) or (f) GDPR).
datenschutz_rights_body: You have the following rights with regard to your personal data: access, rectification, erasure, restriction of processing, objection to processing, and data portability. You also have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority. To exercise your rights, please contact us at the address given above.
practice_report_intro: How long you played, and when. Yours to keep — and to show a teacher, if you have one.
practice_of_which_by_hand: {count} of these you logged by hand.
practice_empty: Nothing here yet for this period. Play something, or add time you spent at the piano.
practice_add_hint: Played at a piano Plinky wasn’t listening to? Put those minutes in yourself.
repertoire_intro: What you are working on, where each piece has got to, and anything you are working toward.
methods_intro: Six things a teacher would suggest, and where in Plinky to do each one.
meta_methods_description: Six ways to practise the piano — chunking, slow practice, hands apart, hearing it first, mixing pieces up and spacing them out — each with the Plinky control that does it.
method_chunking_name: One small piece at a time
method_chunking_how: Pick the two bars that keep going wrong, tap them on the score to set a loop, and play only those until they stop being the hard part.
method_chunking_why: A whole piece practised end to end gives the difficult bar the same few seconds as every other. Looping it gives it all of them.
method_slow_name: Slow enough to get it right
method_slow_how: Drop the tempo until every note lands where you meant it. Move it up a little only once a run goes by cleanly.
method_slow_why: Whatever you play is what you learn, mistakes included. Slow is the speed at which you can choose what that is.
method_hands_apart_how: Set the piece to one hand and let Plinky play the other. Swap. Then put them together.
method_hands_apart_why: Two hands doing different things is two problems at once. Apart, each one is small enough to solve.
method_hearing_first_name: Hear it before you play it
method_hearing_first_how: Listen to the phrase, then turn the noteheads blank and find it by ear.
method_hearing_first_why: Reading tells you which key; hearing tells you whether you got there. The second one is what carries you when the page runs out.
method_interleaving_how: Instead of one piece for half an hour, take a review session and let it hand you a different one each time.
method_interleaving_why: Switching feels worse in the moment and holds far better a week later. The effort of coming back to something is the part that sticks.
method_spacing_how: Let a piece go quiet for a few days, then play it again. Plinky already tracks when each one is ready.
method_spacing_why: Something almost forgotten and then recalled is remembered longer than something never allowed to fade.
assignments_due_hint: A lesson, an exam, a recital — optional.
tools_intro: Things to look up mid-practice. No account, no instrument needed — just the ones you keep reaching for.
learn_intro: Everything Plinky can teach you away from a piece — how the music is built, what its marks mean, and the little things you look up mid-practice.
meta_tools_description: Free piano tools in your browser: a circle of fifths you can hear, a scale and chord explorer shown on the keys, and a tap-tempo reader. No account needed.
tools_circle_hint: The twelve keys in the order a fifth takes you through them. Neighbours differ by a single sharp or flat. Pick one to hear its chord.
tools_scales_hint: Any scale from any note, lit up on the keys.
tools_chords_hint: Any chord from any note, lit up on the keys.
tools_tap_hint: Know how fast it goes but not the number? Tap along and read it off.
theory_intro: Eight short lessons on what a stave is actually telling you. Each one has something to play — read the paragraph, then hear it.
meta_theory_description: A free eight-lesson course in piano theory: reading the stave, sharps and flats, keys and scales, and how chords get their colour. Play each idea in your browser.
theory_outro: That is all {count} of them. The glossary has the marks themselves, and the little tools are there when you want to look something up.
theory_staff_title: A stave is a picture of a keyboard
theory_staff_body: The five lines and the four gaps between them are nine neighbouring white keys. Higher on the page means further right on the piano, and a note sitting one step above another is the very next white key up. That is the whole idea — everything else is a detail on top of it.
theory_steps_body: The smallest move on a piano is to the very next key, black or white: a half step. Two of those make a whole step. A sharp raises a note by a half step and a flat lowers it, which is why the black keys have two names each — the same key, reached from either side.
theory_octave_body: Count twelve keys up from any note, black and white alike, and you land on one that sounds like it again, only higher — an octave. On the white keys that is eight of them, C up to the next C. It is the one interval every ear recognises without being taught, and it is why the keyboard is the same twelve keys repeating rather than eighty-eight different ones.
theory_major_body: Play from C to C on the white keys and you have a major scale: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. That pattern is what makes it sound major, not the notes themselves — start anywhere and keep the pattern and you get the same brightness in a different place.
theory_minor_body: Start on A instead and play the same white keys, and the pattern shifts: the third step is now a half step closer to the first. That one smaller gap is most of what people hear as sad. Same keys, different starting point, different feeling.
theory_signature_body: Keeping the major pattern from a note other than C means some keys have to move. Start on G and the seventh note has to be F sharp, or the pattern breaks. Rather than write that sharp on every F, the key signature says it once at the front — which is all a signature is: the accidentals this piece takes for granted.
theory_triads_body: Take a note, skip one, take the next, skip one, take the next: that is a triad, the chord almost all music is built from. On C it comes out C, E, G. Because you are skipping alternate steps, the shape looks like a snowman on the page — three noteheads stacked with no gaps.
theory_colour_title: Major and minor, one key apart
theory_colour_body: The middle note is the one carrying the mood. Lower it by a half step and a major chord becomes minor. It is a single key's difference and it changes everything you feel about the sound, which is worth hearing rather than reading.
lights_enable: Light the keys I'm about to play
lights_enable_help: For a keyboard whose keys light up. Plinky shows you what's coming next; your reading-aid setting above decides when.
lights_profile_help: Picking one fills in the channels its maker ships. Change them below if you've changed them on the instrument.
lights_test_help: Lights a C major chord in both hands. Nothing happening? Check that key lighting is switched on at the keyboard itself — Casio calls it MIDI In Navigate, Yamaha calls it Light Guide.
